muqaddimah:
بِسْمِ اللَّهِ الرَّحْمَٰنِ الرَّحِيمِ

In the name of Allah, the Most Merciful, the Most Kind

Muqaddimah المقدمة

All praise belongs to Allah. We praise Him, we ask for His help and we seek His forgiveness. We thank Him for His countless blessings, and above all for the greatest gift He has given us: the Noble Qur’an. It is a blessed Book, a guide for all people, a light for our hearts and a healing for what is in our chests.

Allah sent it down to guide His servants. Reciting it brings calm to the soul, reflecting on it brings the heart to life, and living by it brings happiness in this world and the next. In His mercy He made it easy to remember, and He told us how to recite it:

﴿وَرَتِّلِ ٱلۡقُرۡءَانَ تَرۡتِیلًا﴾

“And recite the Qur’an slowly and clearly.” (al-Muzzammil 73:4)

And He promised to protect it Himself:

﴿إِنَّا نَحۡنُ نَزَّلۡنَا ٱلذِّكۡرَ وَإِنَّا لَهُۥ لَحَـٰفِظُونَ﴾

“It is We who sent down the Reminder, and it is We who will protect it.” (al-Hijr 15:9)

I bear witness that there is no god worthy of worship except Allah, alone, with no partner, and that Muhammad ﷺ is His servant and His Messenger. Allah sent the Qur’an down to him, and he recited it to his companions, taught them how to read it and what it means, and raised them to live by it. They carried it in their hearts and passed it on, carefully and faithfully, to those who came after them. May Allah send His peace and blessings upon him, his family, his companions, and everyone who follows them in goodness until the Last Day.

To proceed:

Few deeds are more precious than learning the Qur’an and teaching it. The Prophet ﷺ said:

«خَيْرُكُمْ مَنْ تَعَلَّمَ الْقُرْآنَ وَعَلَّمَهُ»

“The best of you are those who learn the Qur’an and teach it.” (al-Bukhari 5027)

This hadith is the reason for this book. I wanted to help plant a love of the Qur’an in the hearts of our sons and daughters, and to give children and beginners a simple, clear way to learn the rules of tajweed and to recite the Book of Allah well.

The book is built on Tuhfat al-Atfal wal-Ghilman fi Tajwid al-Qur’an, the well-known poem by Shaykh Sulayman ibn Husayn al-Jamzuri, may Allah have mercy on him. I chose it because it is well ordered and short, and it gathers the rules a beginner needs most.

I did not want children only to memorise the lines and learn the names of the rules. I wanted them to understand the rules and use them. So every rule comes with examples from the Qur’an, with the letters of the rule shown in colour, so that students can find the rules in the words of Allah and practise reading them correctly.

Tajweed is not about memorising terms. Its purpose is to recite the Qur’an beautifully, with respect for it, thinking about its meanings and acting on what it teaches.

Please remember that everything in this book, the rules and the examples, should be studied with a qualified teacher who recites well and knows tajweed. This knowledge has always been passed on face to face: the student listens, recites and is corrected. Reading on your own is not enough. This book is a helper for learning and revision, not a replacement for a good teacher.

A word to teachers and parents

To teachers: please teach these rules gently and patiently, one step at a time, keeping in mind each child’s age and ability. Let the children hear the correct recitation, practise it and revise it often. Correct their mistakes kindly and with plenty of encouragement, so that learning the Qur’an becomes something they enjoy, not something they dread.

To parents: stay close to your children’s learning. Set aside a few minutes every day to revise with them and encourage them, and keep in touch with their teacher so you know what they need to practise. Be careful not to push them beyond what they can manage.

When teachers and families work together, patiently and steadily, the knowledge settles, the recitation improves, and love of the Qur’an grows in young hearts.

My hope is that this small work helps raise a generation that loves the Book of Allah, recites it well, reflects on it and lives by it, so that the Qur’an becomes a light in their hearts, a guide in their lives, and a means of success in this world and the next.

This is a human effort, and it will have shortcomings. Whatever is right in it is from the grace of Allah, and whatever is wrong is from me; I ask Allah to forgive me. If you find a mistake, I would be grateful if you let me know. Good advice is always welcome, and returning to what is right is a virtue.

I ask Allah, the Most Generous, to accept this work, to make it sincerely for His sake, and to make it useful to students, teachers and parents. May He write a lasting reward through it for us and for our parents, and make it beneficial knowledge and an ongoing charity.

The Prophet ﷺ said:

«إِنَّ لِلَّهِ أَهْلِينَ مِنَ النَّاسِ». قَالُوا: يَا رَسُولَ اللَّهِ، مَنْ هُمْ؟ قَالَ: «هُمْ أَهْلُ الْقُرْآنِ، أَهْلُ اللَّهِ وَخَاصَّتُهُ»

“Allah has His own people among mankind.” They asked, “O Messenger of Allah, who are they?” He said, “The people of the Qur’an. They are the people of Allah and His chosen ones.” (Ibn Majah 215)

اللَّهُمَّ اجْعَلْنَا وَذُرِّيَّاتِنَا مِنْ أَهْلِ الْقُرْآنِ الَّذِينَ هُمْ أَهْلُكَ وَخَاصَّتُكَ، وَاجْعَلِ الْقُرْآنَ الْعَظِيمَ رَبِيعَ قُلُوبِنَا وَنُورَ صُدُورِنَا.

“O Allah, make us and our children among the people of the Qur’an, who are Your people and Your chosen ones, and make the Mighty Qur’an the spring of our hearts and the light of our chests.”

And may Allah send His peace and blessings upon our Prophet Muhammad ﷺ, his family and all his companions.

Feysel Reshid

فَيْصَل رَشِيد

chapters.title: Meet the Poem
chapters.intro: Before the rules, Imam al-Jamzuri introduces himself, praises Allah, and tells us what his poem is about.

lessons.title: The Author Begins
explain: The poem is written by Imam Sulayman al-Jamzuri, a teacher of the Qur'an in Egypt who lived about 250 years ago. He begins by calling himself someone who is always hoping for the mercy of Allah, the Most Forgiving.
Then he does what every good Muslim writer does at the start: he praises Allah and sends blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, his family and everyone who recites the Qur'an.
That includes you! Every time you recite, you are one of the people he made du'a for.
lessons.remember: Start every good thing with praising Allah and sending blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.

examples.note: The poem begins with “al-hamdu lillah”, just like the Qur'an.

lessons.title: A Gift for Children
explain: He tells us his poem is for the student who wants to learn three big topics: the rules of noon sakinah and tanween, and the rules of madd (stretching).
He named it Tuhfat al-Atfal, “A Gift for Children”, and he learned it from his teacher, Shaykh al-Mihi.
He hopes it will benefit students, and that Allah will accept it and reward him. We say “Amin”, and we learn it so that it benefits us too.
lessons.remember: Tajweed means reciting every letter correctly, the way the Prophet ﷺ recited.

examples.note: Allah tells us: “Recite the Qur'an with tartil”, slowly and correctly.

chapters.title: Noon Sakinah and Tanween
chapters.intro: A noon with sukun (نْ) and tanween (ـًـٍـٌ) both make an “n” sound. What happens to that sound depends on the letter that comes next.

lessons.title: Four Rules
explain: A noon sakinah is a noon with a sukun on it: نْ. Tanween is the double harakah at the end of a word: ـً ـٍ ـٌ. When you say tanween, it sounds like a hidden noon: “-an, -in, -un”.
So the poem treats them together. When a noon sakinah or tanween is followed by another letter, there are four things that can happen: Izhar, Idgham, Iqlab and Ikhfa.
Which one? It all depends on the letter that comes straight after. Learn the letters, and you know the rule!
lessons.remember: Look at the letter AFTER the noon sakinah or tanween. That letter decides the rule.

examples.note: Izhar: the noon is clear before خ.
Idgham with ghunnah: the noon merges into ي.
Iqlab: the noon becomes a meem sound before ب.
Ikhfa: the noon is hidden before ش.

challenge.task: Find every noon sakinah and tanween in this ayah. Write each word and its rule.
challenge.html: ٱلَّذِیۤ أَطۡعَمَهُم مِّن جُوعࣲ وَءَامَنَهُم مِّنۡ خَوۡفِۭ

lessons.title: Izhar: Say It Clearly
explain: The first rule is Izhar, which means “making clear”. If a noon sakinah or tanween comes before one of the six throat letters, you say the noon clearly, without any ghunnah (nasal humming).
The six throat letters are: ء هـ ع ح غ خ. They are called throat letters because they come from the throat, which is far from where we say noon. Because they are far apart, the noon stays clear.
It can happen inside one word, or between two words.
lessons.remember: Throat letters ء هـ ع ح غ خ → say the noon clearly.
lessons.how: Say the noon, stop on it cleanly, then say the throat letter.

examples.note: Noon then ع in the same word: an‘amta.
Noon then خ across two words: min khawf.

challenge.task: Find the tanween that is read with Izhar. Which throat letter comes after it?

lessons.title: Idgham: Merging
explain: The second rule is Idgham, which means “merging”. The noon sakinah or tanween disappears into the next letter, as if the two became one letter with a shaddah.
Idgham happens with six letters, which are gathered in the word يَرْمَلُونَ (yarmalun): ي ر م ل و ن.
Idgham only happens between two words: the noon at the end of one word, and the yarmalun letter at the start of the next.
lessons.remember: Yarmalun letters ي ر م ل و ن → merge the noon into them.

challenge.task: Find the TWO places where noon sakinah or tanween merges. Is each one with or without ghunnah?
challenge.html: یُسۡقَوۡنَ مِن رَّحِیقࣲ مَّخۡتُومٍ

lessons.title: Idgham with Ghunnah
explain: Idgham has two kinds. The first is Idgham with ghunnah: the noon merges into the next letter, but you keep a nasal humming sound (ghunnah) for 2 counts.
This happens with four letters, gathered in the word يَنْمُو (yanmu): ي ن م و.
Listen to your teacher: the noon disappears, but its ghunnah stays, flowing into the next letter.
lessons.remember: Yanmu letters ي ن م و → merge WITH ghunnah (2 counts).
lessons.how: Don't say the noon. Go straight to the next letter, humming through the nose for 2 counts.

challenge.task: This ayah has TWO Idghams with ghunnah. Find them both.
challenge.html: فَمَن یَعۡمَلۡ مِثۡقَالَ ذَرَّةٍ خَیۡرࣰا یَرَهُۥ

lessons.title: Not Inside One Word!
explain: There is an exception. If the noon sakinah and the yanmu letter are together inside ONE word, there is no idgham. You read the noon clearly.
In the whole Qur'an, this happens in only four words: الدُّنْيَا (ad-dunya), قِنْوَانٌ (qinwan), صِنْوَانٌ (sinwan) and بُنْيَانٌ (bunyan).
If we merged them, the words would sound like different words, and the meaning would be lost. So we keep the noon clear. This is called Izhar Mutlaq.
lessons.remember: Noon + yanmu letter in ONE word → no merging. Say the noon clearly.

examples.note: ad-dunya: noon then ي in one word.
sinwan: noon then و in one word.
qinwan: noon then و in one word.
bunyan: noon then ي in one word.

challenge.task: One word has a noon sakinah and a ya in the SAME word. Find it. Is there idgham?

answers.label: No idgham: Izhar, because it is one word

lessons.title: Idgham Without Ghunnah
explain: The second kind of idgham is without ghunnah. It happens with two letters only: ل (lam) and ر (ra).
The noon sakinah or tanween disappears completely into the lam or ra, with no humming at all. The lam or ra is said as if it has a shaddah.
The poem says “repeat it well”, because this needs practice to sound smooth.
lessons.remember: ل and ر → merge completely, NO ghunnah.
lessons.how: Skip the noon and say the lam or ra with a shaddah.

challenge.task: Find the Idgham without ghunnah.

lessons.title: Iqlab: Changing
explain: The third rule is Iqlab, which means “changing”. It happens with only ONE letter: ب (ba).
When a noon sakinah or tanween comes before ب, the noon sound changes into a hidden meem sound, with ghunnah for 2 counts.
In many copies of the Qur'an, you will see a small meem (ۢ) written above the noon or tanween to remind you.
lessons.remember: ب → change the noon into a hidden meem, with ghunnah.
lessons.how: Close your lips gently for a meem, hum for 2 counts, then say ب.

challenge.task: Find the Iqlab. Where does the noon turn into a meem sound?

lessons.title: Ikhfa: Hiding
explain: The fourth rule is Ikhfa, which means “hiding”. It happens with all the letters that are left: fifteen letters.
With ikhfa, the noon is not said clearly, and it is not merged either. It is somewhere in between: hidden, with ghunnah for 2 counts. Your tongue gets ready for the next letter while you hum.
Ikhfa is a duty (wajib) for every reciter, so practise it carefully with a teacher.
lessons.remember: The other 15 letters → hide the noon, with ghunnah (2 counts).
lessons.how: Don't touch the noon with your tongue. Hum through the nose, then say the next letter.

challenge.task: Find the Ikhfa.

lessons.title: The Fifteen Ikhfa Letters
explain: This clever line is a memory code. The FIRST letter of each word is one of the 15 ikhfa letters:
صِفْ ذَا ثَنَا كَمْ جَادَ شَخْصٌ قَدْ سَمَا دُمْ طَيِّبًا زِدْ فِي تُقًى ضَعْ ظَالِمَا  →  ص ذ ث ك ج ش ق س د ط ز ف ت ض ظ

It even has a nice meaning: “Describe the praiseworthy person: how generous he is, he has risen high. Stay good, grow in taqwa, and leave the wrongdoer.” The table shows one Qur'an word for every ikhfa letter.
lessons.remember: The first letters of “Sif dha thana…” are the 15 ikhfa letters.

challenge.task: Find the Ikhfa. Which of the fifteen letters comes after the noon?

quiz: ء هـ ع ح غ خ
ي ر م ل و ن
In which word are the letters of Idgham gathered?
What happens before the letter ب?
Why is there no idgham in الدُّنْيَا?
Because it is a short word
Because the noon and ي are in one word
Because ي is a throat letter

chapters.title: Meem and Noon with Shaddah
chapters.intro: Whenever you see a noon or a meem with a shaddah (نّ مّ), there is always a ghunnah.

lessons.title: Letters of Ghunnah
explain: A ghunnah is a beautiful humming sound that comes from the nose. Try holding your nose while saying “nnn”: the sound stops! That shows you where ghunnah comes from.
Whenever a noon or a meem has a shaddah (نّ or مّ), you must make a ghunnah for 2 counts. Each one is called a “letter of ghunnah”.
Some of the most common words in the Qur'an have this: إِنَّ, ثُمَّ and النَّاسِ.
lessons.remember: نّ and مّ → always ghunnah, 2 counts.
lessons.how: Hold the noon or meem and hum through the nose for 2 counts.

challenge.task: Find the meem or noon with a shaddah. How long is its ghunnah?

quiz: Where does the sound of ghunnah come from?
How long is the ghunnah of نّ and مّ?
Which word has a noon with shaddah?

chapters.title: Meem Sakinah
chapters.intro: A meem with sukun (مْ) also has rules. There are only three, and they are easier than the noon rules.

lessons.title: Three Rules for Meem
explain: A meem sakinah is a meem with a sukun: مْ. It can come before any letter of the alphabet, except the soft alif (an alif with no harakah), because a sukun can never be followed by a sukun.
Meem sakinah has three rules only: Ikhfa (hiding), Idgham (merging) and Izhar (clear). Just like noon, the letter that comes next decides the rule.
Because meem is said with the lips, these rules are called “shafawi”, which means “of the lips”.
lessons.remember: Meem sakinah: Ikhfa, Idgham or Izhar. Look at the next letter.

challenge.task: Find the TWO meem sakinahs. Write the rule for each one.
challenge.html: أَلَمۡ یَعۡلَم بِأَنَّ ٱللَّهَ یَرَىٰ

lessons.title: Ikhfa Shafawi
explain: The first rule: if a meem sakinah comes before ب (ba), the meem is hidden, with a ghunnah for 2 counts.
Your lips touch very lightly, and you hum, before you say the ب. It is called Ikhfa Shafawi, the ikhfa of the lips.
lessons.remember: مْ + ب → hide the meem with ghunnah.
lessons.how: Touch your lips together very lightly, hum for 2 counts, then say ب.

challenge.task: Find the Ikhfa shafawi.

lessons.title: Idgham Shafawi
explain: The second rule: if a meem sakinah comes before another meem, the two meems merge into one meem with a shaddah, with ghunnah for 2 counts.
Because two of the SAME letter meet, it is called Idgham Mithlayn Saghir (the small merging of two identical letters), or simply Idgham Shafawi.
lessons.remember: مْ + م → merge into one meem with ghunnah.

challenge.task: Find the Idgham shafawi.

lessons.title: Izhar Shafawi
explain: The third rule: before all the other letters (everything except ب and م), the meem sakinah is said clearly, with no ghunnah. This is Izhar Shafawi.

Imam al-Jamzuri gives a special warning: be extra careful before و (waw) and ف (fa). The meem is close to ف (both use the lips) and the same place as و, so lazy reciters accidentally hide the meem. Don't! Keep it clear.
lessons.remember: All other letters → say the meem clearly. Take care before و and ف!
lessons.how: Close your lips firmly on the meem, then open them for the next letter.

challenge.task: Find the Izhar shafawi.

quiz: What happens when مْ comes before ب?
Before which two letters must you take extra care to keep the meem clear?

chapters.title: The Lam of “Al” and the Lam of Verbs
chapters.intro: The word “al” (the) has a lam. Sometimes you say it, and sometimes it disappears. The letter after it decides.

lessons.title: Lam Qamariyyah: The Moon Letters
explain: The lam of “al” has two states. The first is Izhar: you say the lam clearly, with a sukun.
This happens before fourteen letters, gathered in the phrase اِبْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ (“seek your Hajj and fear that it is not accepted”): ا ب غ ح ج ك و خ ف ع ق ي م هـ.
These are called the Moon letters, because in اَلْقَمَرُ (the moon) the lam is clear.
lessons.remember: Moon letters → say the lam: al-qamar, al-hamd.

challenge.task: Find the Lam Qamariyyah (the lam you can hear).

lessons.title: Lam Shamsiyyah: The Sun Letters
explain: The second state is Idgham: the lam disappears, and the next letter gets a shaddah. It happens with the other fourteen letters.
Their memory code is the line طِبْ ثُمَّ صِلْ رُحْمًا تَفُزْ ضِفْ ذَا نِعَمْ دَعْ سُوءَ ظَنٍّ زُرْ شَرِيفًا لِلْكَرَمْ. Take the first letter of each word: ط ث ص ر ت ض ذ ن د س ظ ز ش ل.
These are the Sun letters, because in اَلشَّمْسُ (the sun) the lam is silent: “ash-shams”.
lessons.remember: Sun letters → the lam is silent and the next letter has shaddah: ash-shams, an-nas.
lessons.how: Skip the lam. Go from the alif straight to the letter with shaddah.

challenge.task: Find the Lam Shamsiyyah (the lam you cannot hear).

lessons.title: The Lam of a Verb
explain: The poem now talks about a different lam: the lam that is part of a verb (an action word). This lam is ALWAYS said clearly, whatever letter comes after it.
The poem gives three examples: قُلْ نَعَمْ (“say: yes”), قُلْنَا (“We said”) and الْتَقَى (“they met”).
Only one exception: if the next letter is also lam or ra, it merges (as in قُل رَّبِّ), which you will learn in the next chapter.
lessons.remember: The lam of a verb is always clear: qul na‘am, qulna, iltaqa.

challenge.task: Find the lam of a verb. Is it said clearly?

answers.label: Lam of a verb: said clearly (Izhar)

quiz: In اَلْقَمَرُ, is the lam said or silent?
In اَلشَّمْسُ, is the lam said or silent?
How many Sun letters are there?
The lam in قُلْ نَعَمْ is:
Clear, because it is the lam of a verb

chapters.title: Two Letters Meeting
chapters.intro: When two letters meet, scholars give the meeting a name, depending on how alike the two letters are.

lessons.title: Identical, Close and Related
explain: Every letter has a makhraj (where it comes from in the mouth) and sifat (qualities).
Mithlayn (identical): two of the same letter, like ب and ب.
Mutajanisayn (related): same place in the mouth, different qualities, like ت and د, or ذ and ظ.
Mutaqaribayn (close): their places are near each other, like ل and ر.
lessons.remember: Same letter = mithlayn. Same place = mutajanisayn. Near place = mutaqaribayn.

examples.note: Mithlayn: ب meets ب, and they merge.
Mutajanisayn: د meets ت, and they merge.
Mutajanisayn: ذ meets ظ, and they merge.
Mutaqaribayn: ل meets ر, and they merge.

challenge.task: Find two letters that are the SAME meeting each other. What is this meeting called?
challenge.html: فَقُلۡ هَل لَّكَ إِلَىٰۤ أَن تَزَكَّىٰ

lessons.title: Small and Large
explain: Each kind of meeting can be small (saghir) or large (kabir).
Saghir (small): the first letter has a sukun and the second has a harakah. This is where merging (idgham) usually happens, as in the examples on the last page.
Kabir (large): both letters have a harakah. In the way we recite (Hafs), these are said clearly, one after the other. The poem says: understand them through examples!
lessons.remember: First letter with sukun = small (usually merged). Both with harakah = large (said clearly).

examples.note: Small mithlayn: دْ then د, merged.
Large mithlayn: هِ then هُ, both said clearly.
Large mithlayn: كَ then كُ, both said clearly.

challenge.task: Find two identical letters side by side that BOTH have a harakah. Small or large?
challenge.html: مَا سَلَكَكُمۡ فِی سَقَرَ

quiz: Two of the same letter meeting is called:
ت and د come from the same place. They are:
When both letters have a harakah, the meeting is:

chapters.title: Madd: Stretching
chapters.intro: Madd means stretching a sound. Some madd is always 2 counts, and some is longer, because of something that comes after it.

lessons.title: Natural Madd
explain: Madd has two main kinds: asli (original) and far‘i (extra). The asli madd is also called tabi‘i, natural madd.
Natural madd does not need any reason (sabab) to happen. Without it, the madd letter would not even exist! It is stretched for 2 counts.
How do you know it is natural madd? Look at the letter after the madd letter: if it is NOT a hamzah and NOT a sukun, the madd is natural.
lessons.remember: A madd letter with no hamzah or sukun after it → 2 counts.
lessons.how: Count 2 at the speed of a gentle finger tap: 1, 2.

challenge.task: Find THREE words with a natural madd (2 counts).
challenge.html: مَا وَدَّعَكَ رَبُّكَ وَمَا قَلَىٰ

lessons.title: Extra Madd
explain: The second kind is far‘i, the extra madd. It is longer than 2 counts, and it always has a reason (sabab).
There are two reasons: a hamzah (ء) or a sukun that comes after the madd letter.
You will meet all the kinds of extra madd in the next chapter.
lessons.remember: Extra madd = a madd letter + a hamzah or a sukun.

examples.note: ad-dallin: madd then a sukun (in the shaddah).

challenge.task: Find the TWO madds that are longer than 2 counts. What is the reason for each one?
challenge.html: فَإِذَا جَاۤءَتِ ٱلصَّاۤخَّةُ

answers.label: A hamzah after it: Madd muttasil, 4 or 5
A sukun (shaddah) after it: Madd lazim, 6

lessons.title: The Three Madd Letters
explain: There are three madd letters: و ا ي. The poem gathers them in the word وَايْ (way), and shows all three in the Qur'an word نُوحِيهَا (nuhiha).
Each madd letter has a condition. The letter before it must have the matching harakah:
ا after a fathah ـَا   ·   و with sukun after a dammah ـُو   ·   ي with sukun after a kasrah ـِي
lessons.remember: Fathah → alif. Dammah → waw. Kasrah → ya.

examples.note: nuhiha: all three madd letters in one word!

challenge.task: Find the madd letters: alif after a fathah, waw after a dammah and ya after a kasrah.
challenge.html: ٱلَّذِینَ هُمۡ عَن صَلَاتِهِمۡ سَاهُونَ

answers.label: Alif, then waw after a dammah

lessons.title: The Soft Letters: Leen
explain: Two letters can be soft (leen): و and ي when they have a sukun and the letter before them has a FATHAH.
They are not madd letters, but they have a softness. When you stop on a word with a leen letter, you may stretch it a little (2, 4 or 6 counts).
Surah Quraysh has beautiful examples.
lessons.remember: وْ or يْ after a fathah = leen.

examples.note: quraysh: ya sakinah after a fathah.
khawf: waw sakinah after a fathah.

challenge.task: Find the TWO leen letters (a waw or ya with sukun after a fathah).

quiz: What are the two reasons for extra madd?
Which Qur'an word has all three madd letters?
A waw with sukun after a FATHAH is a:

chapters.title: The Rulings of Madd
chapters.intro: Madd has three rulings: wajib (required), ja'iz (allowed) and lazim (always necessary).

lessons.title: Wajib: Madd Muttasil
explain: The three rulings of madd are: wajib (required), ja'iz (allowed, with a choice) and lazim (always necessary).
Madd is wajib when a hamzah comes after a madd letter in the SAME word. It is called Muttasil, “joined”, because the madd and the hamzah are joined in one word.
It is stretched for 4 or 5 counts. All the reciters agree that it must be stretched more than 2.
lessons.remember: Madd + hamzah in ONE word → 4 or 5 counts (required).

challenge.task: Find the TWO Madd muttasil (madd letter and hamzah in the same word).
challenge.html: جَزَاۤءࣰ مِّن رَّبِّكَ عَطَاۤءً حِسَابࣰا

lessons.title: Ja'iz: Madd Munfasil
explain: Madd is ja'iz (allowed) when the madd letter is at the end of one word, and the hamzah is at the start of the next word. It is called Munfasil, “separated”.
In the recitation of Hafs by way of ash-Shatibiyyah, it is stretched 4 or 5 counts. Some ways of reciting allow it shorter. That is why it is called “allowed”.
Whatever length your teacher teaches you, keep it the same every time.
lessons.remember: Madd at the end of a word + hamzah at the start of the next → 4 or 5 counts.

challenge.task: Find the Madd munfasil (madd letter at the end of a word, hamzah at the start of the next).

lessons.title: Madd Because of Stopping
explain: Another kind of ja'iz madd happens when you STOP on a word. The last letter gets a sukun because you stopped, and if a madd letter is just before it, you may stretch it.
The poem's examples are تَعْلَمُونَ and نَسْتَعِينُ. When you stop on them, you say ta‘lamun and nasta‘in.
This is called ‘Arid li-s-Sukun (madd because of a passing sukun). You may stretch it 2, 4 or 6 counts.
lessons.remember: Stopping after a madd letter → 2, 4 or 6 counts.

challenge.task: Stop at the end of this ayah. Which word gets a madd because you stopped?

lessons.title: Madd Badal
explain: Madd Badal happens when the hamzah comes BEFORE the madd letter, in the same word.
The poem's examples are آمَنُوا (they believed) and إِيمَانًا (faith).
In Hafs, Madd Badal is stretched for 2 counts only, just like natural madd.
lessons.remember: Hamzah BEFORE a madd letter → Madd Badal, 2 counts in Hafs.

challenge.task: Find the Madd badal (a hamzah BEFORE the madd letter).
challenge.html: إِنَّ هَـٰذَا لَفِی ٱلصُّحُفِ ٱلۡأُولَىٰ

lessons.title: Lazim: Always Six
explain: The third ruling is lazim, “always necessary”. It happens when a madd letter is followed by a permanent sukun: a sukun that stays whether you stop or keep reading.
Madd Lazim is ALWAYS stretched for 6 counts. Every reciter agrees.
The most famous example is at the end of Surah al-Fatihah: وَلَا الضَّالِّينَ.
lessons.remember: Madd letter + permanent sukun → always 6 counts.

challenge.task: Find the Madd lazim. How many counts?

quiz: Madd and hamzah in the same word is:
Madd at the end of one word and hamzah at the start of the next is:
In Madd Badal, the hamzah comes:

chapters.title: Madd Lazim and the Opening Letters
chapters.intro: Madd Lazim comes in four types, and some of them are found in the special letters at the start of some surahs.

lessons.title: Four Types of Madd Lazim
explain: Madd Lazim is either Kalimi (in a word) or Harfi (in a letter). And each one is either Muthaqqal (heavy, with a shaddah) or Mukhaffaf (light, just a sukun). That makes four types.
Kalimi: the madd letter and the sukun are in a normal word. Harfi: they are in the name of an opening letter that has three sounds with a madd in the middle, like “meem” (م ي م) or “lam” (ل ا م).
Muthaqqal: there is an idgham (a shaddah after the madd). Mukhaffaf: there is no idgham, just a sukun.
lessons.remember: Kalimi or Harfi × Muthaqqal or Mukhaffaf = 4 types. All are 6 counts.

examples.note: Kalimi Muthaqqal: in a word, with shaddah.
Kalimi Mukhaffaf: aal'ana, in a word, just a sukun.
Harfi: alif-laaam-meeem. Laam merges into meem (muthaqqal), meem is light (mukhaffaf).

challenge.task: Say the names of these three letters. Which has no madd? Which is heavy (muthaqqal)? Which is light (mukhaffaf)?

answers.label: Alif: no madd · Lam: harfi muthaqqal · Meem: harfi mukhaffaf

lessons.title: Kam ‘Asal Naqas
explain: Madd Lazim Harfi is only found in the opening letters of some surahs, and only in eight letters. They are gathered in the phrase كَمْ عَسَلْ نَقَصْ: ك م ع س ل ن ق ص.
Each of these letters' names has three sounds with a madd in the middle: kaaf, meem, ‘ayn, seen, laam, noon, qaaf, saad. They are stretched for 6 counts.
The letter ‘ayn (in كٓهيعٓصٓ and عٓسٓقٓ) is special: you may stretch it 4 or 6 counts, but 6 is preferred.
lessons.remember: Kam ‘asal naqas letters → 6 counts. ‘Ayn: 4 or 6 (6 is better).

challenge.task: Which of these opening letters are from كَمْ عَسَلْ نَقَصْ? How long is each one?

answers.label: Kaf and Sad: 6 counts · ‘Ayn: 4 or 6 (6 is better)

lessons.title: Hayyun Tahir: Two Counts
explain: Some opening letters have only TWO sounds in their names: ha (حا), ya (يا), ta (طا), ha (ها), ra (را). They are stretched with natural madd, 2 counts.
They are gathered in the phrase حَيٌّ طَاهِرٌ (hayyun tahir): ح ي ط هـ ر.
And alif (ا) at the start of الٓمٓ has no madd at all, because its name (alif) has no madd letter in the middle.
lessons.remember: Hayyun tahir letters → 2 counts. Alif → no madd.

examples.note: ya-seen: ya is 2 counts, seen is 6.
ha-meem: ha is 2 counts, meem is 6.

challenge.task: Which letter is from حَيٌّ طَاهِرٌ and is read with only 2 counts?

lessons.title: The Fourteen Opening Letters
explain: Altogether, fourteen different letters appear at the openings of the surahs. They are gathered in the phrase صِلْهُ سُحَيْرًا مَنْ قَطَعَكْ (“join him at dawn, the one who cut you off”).
ص ل هـ س ح ي ر ا م ن ق ط ع ك
What a beautiful meaning to end the rules with: keep good ties with people, even the ones who are unkind to you.
lessons.remember: “Silhu suhayran man qata‘ak” gathers all 14 opening letters.

challenge.task: Name both opening letters and say how long each one stretches.

quiz: Which phrase gathers the 8 letters of Madd Lazim Harfi?

chapters.title: The End of the Poem
chapters.intro: Imam al-Jamzuri finishes his gift with praise of Allah and blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.

lessons.title: Praise and Blessings
explain: The poem is complete, and the Imam praises Allah for helping him finish it.

He hides two numbers in Arabic letters (an old way of counting called abjad). نَدٌّ بَدَا (nadd bada) adds up to 61, the number of lines. بُشْرَى لِمَنْ يُتْقِنُهَا (good news for whoever masters it) adds up to 1198, the year he finished it (about 1784 CE).
He ends, just as he began, with blessings on the Prophet ﷺ, his family, his companions, everyone who follows them, every reciter and every listener. That means you!
lessons.remember: End every good work as you began it: with praise of Allah and blessings on the Prophet ﷺ.

examples.html: یَـٰۤأَیُّهَا ٱلَّذِینَ ءَامَنُوا۟ صَلُّوا۟ عَلَیۡهِ وَسَلِّمُوا۟ تَسۡلِیمًا
examples.plain: یَـٰۤأَیُّهَا ٱلَّذِینَ ءَامَنُوا۟ صَلُّوا۟ عَلَیۡهِ وَسَلِّمُوا۟ تَسۡلِیمًا
examples.note: Allah tells us to send blessings and peace on the Prophet ﷺ.

izhar: Clear: say the letter clearly, no ghunnah
iqlab: Change the noon to a hidden meem, with ghunnah
ikhfa: Hide the noon or meem, with ghunnah
shams: The lam is silent; the next letter has shaddah
maddx: Stretch for 4 or 5 counts (or 2–6 where allowed)
leen: A soft waw or ya after a fathah
letter: The letter we are looking at

1.ar: يَقُولُ رَاجِي رَحْمَةِ الْغَفُورِ دَوْمًا سُلَيْمَانُ هُوَ الْجَمْزُورِي
1.en: Sulayman al-Jamzuri says, while always hoping for the mercy of the Most Forgiving.

2.ar: الْحَمْدُ لِلَّهِ مُصَلِّيًا عَلَى مُحَمَّدٍ وَآلِهِ وَمَنْ تَلَا
2.en: All praise is for Allah, with prayers upon Muhammad ﷺ, his family, and those who follow and recite.

3.ar: وَبَعْدُ هَذَا النَّظْمُ لِلْمُرِيدِ فِي النُّونِ وَالتَّنْوِينِ وَالْمُدُودِ
3.en: Thereafter, this poem is for the learner studying Noon, Tanween, and the rules of Madd.

4.ar: سَمَّيْتُهُ بِتُحْفَةِ الْأَطْفَالِ عَنْ شَيْخِنَا الْمِيهِيِّ ذِي الْكَمَالِ
4.en: I named it “A Gift for Children,” transmitted from our accomplished teacher al-Meehi.

5.ar: أَرْجُو بِهِ أَنْ يَنْفَعَ الطُّلَّابَا وَالْأَجْرَ وَالْقَبُولَ وَالثَّوَابَا
5.en: I hope it benefits the students and brings reward, acceptance, and recompense.

6.ar: لِلنُّونِ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ وَلِلتَّنْوِينِ أَرْبَعُ أَحْكَامٍ فَخُذْ تَبْيِينِي
6.en: Noon Sakinah and Tanween have four rules, so take my clear explanation.

7.ar: فَالْأَوَّلُ الْإِظْهَارُ قَبْلَ أَحْرُفٍ لِلْحَلْقِ سِتٌّ رُتِّبَتْ فَلْتَعْرِفِ
7.en: The first rule is Izhar before six throat letters, arranged so that you may know them.

8.ar: هَمْزٌ فَهَاءٌ ثُمَّ عَيْنٌ حَاءُ مُهْمَلَتَانِ ثُمَّ غَيْنٌ خَاءُ
8.en: They are Hamzah, Ha, Ayn, Ha, then Ghayn and Kha.

9.ar: وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِسِتَّةٍ أَتَتْ فِي يَرْمَلُونَ عِنْدَهُمْ قَدْ ثَبَتَتْ
9.en: The second rule is Idgham with six letters gathered in the word Yarmalun.

10.ar: لَكِنَّهَا قِسْمَانِ قِسْمٌ يُدْغَمَا فِيهِ بِغُنَّةٍ بِيَنْمُو عُلِمَا
10.en: Idgham has two types; one is merging with Ghunnah in the letters of Yanmu.

11.ar: إِلَّا إِذَا كَانَا بِكِلْمَةٍ فَلَا تُدْغِمْ كَدُنْيَا ثُمَّ صِنْوَانٍ تَلَا
11.en: But when the letters meet inside one word, do not merge, as in Dunya and Sinwan.

12.ar: وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِغَيْرِ غُنَّةٍ فِي اللَّامِ وَالرَّا ثُمَّ كَرِّرَنَّهْ
12.en: The second type is Idgham without Ghunnah with Lam and Ra; repeat it well.

13.ar: وَالثَّالِثُ الْإِقْلَابُ عِنْدَ الْبَاءِ مِيمًا بِغُنَّةٍ مَعَ الْإِخْفَاءِ
13.en: The third rule is Iqlab before Ba: change the sound to a hidden Meem with Ghunnah.

14.ar: وَالرَّابِعُ الْإِخْفَاءُ عِنْدَ الْفَاضِلِ مِنَ الْحُرُوفِ وَاجِبٌ لِلْفَاضِلِ
14.en: The fourth rule is Ikhfa with the remaining letters, a required rule for the skilled reciter.

15.ar: فِي خَمْسَةٍ مِنْ بَعْدِ عَشْرٍ رَمْزُهَا فِي كِلْمِ هَذَا الْبَيْتِ قَدْ ضَمَّنْتُهَا
15.en: It occurs with fifteen letters whose initials are gathered in the next line.

16.ar: صِفْ ذَا ثَنَا كَمْ جَادَ شَخْصٌ قَدْ سَمَا دُمْ طَيِّبًا زِدْ فِي تُقًى ضَعْ ظَالِمَا
16.en: “Describe a praiseworthy person: how generous he is, he has risen high. Stay good, grow in taqwa, leave the wrongdoer.” The first letter of each word is one of the 15 ikhfa letters.

17.ar: وَغُنَّ مِيمًا ثُمَّ نُونًا شُدِّدَا وَسَمِّ كُلًّا حَرْفَ غُنَّةٍ بَدَا
17.en: Make Ghunnah on a Meem and Noon with Shaddah, and call each a Ghunnah letter.

18.ar: وَالْمِيمُ إِنْ تَسْكُنْ تَجِي قَبْلَ الْهِجَا لَا أَلِفٍ لَيِّنَةٍ لِذِي الْحِجَا
18.en: A Meem Sakinah comes before the alphabet, except a soft Alif, for the person of understanding.

19.ar: أَحْكَامُهَا ثَلَاثَةٌ لِمَنْ ضَبَطْ إِخْفَاءٌ ادْغَامٌ وَإِظْهَارٌ فَقَطْ
19.en: Its rules are three only: Ikhfa, Idgham, and Izhar.

20.ar: فَالْأَوَّلُ الْإِخْفَاءُ عِنْدَ الْبَاءِ وَسَمِّهِ الشَّفَوِيَّ لِلْقُرَّاءِ
20.en: The first is Ikhfa before Ba; call it Ikhfa Shafawi for the reciters.

21.ar: وَالثَّانِ إِدْغَامٌ بِمِثْلِهَا أَتَى وَسَمِّ إِدْغَامًا صَغِيرًا يَا فَتَى
21.en: The second is Idgham into another Meem; call it small Idgham, young learner.

22.ar: وَالثَّالِثُ الْإِظْهَارُ فِي الْبَقِيَّةْ مِنْ أَحْرُفٍ وَسَمِّهَا شَفَوِيَّةْ
22.en: The third is Izhar with all the remaining letters; call it Izhar Shafawi.

23.ar: وَاحْذَرْ لَدَى وَاوٍ وَفَا أَنْ تَخْتَفِي لِقُرْبِهَا وَالِاتِّحَادِ فَاعْرِفِ
23.en: Take care before Waw and Fa that the Meem does not become hidden because of their closeness.

24.ar: لِلَامِ أَلْ حَالَانِ قَبْلَ الْأَحْرُفِ أُولَاهُمَا إِظْهَارُهَا فَلْتَعْرِفِ
24.en: The Lam of Al has two states before the letters; the first is clear pronunciation, so learn it.

25.ar: قَبْلَ ارْبَعٍ مَعْ عَشْرَةٍ خُذْ عِلْمَهُ مِنِ ابْغِ حَجَّكَ وَخَفْ عَقِيمَهُ
25.en: Before fourteen letters. Take their knowledge from “ibghi hajjaka wa khaf ‘aqimah” (seek your Hajj, and fear that it is not accepted).

26.ar: ثَانِيهِمَا إِدْغَامُهَا فِي أَرْبَعٍ وَعَشْرَةٍ أَيْضًا وَرَمْزُهَا فَعِ
26.en: The second state is merging it into the other fourteen letters. Learn their code:

27.ar: طِبْ ثُمَّ صِلْ رُحْمًا تَفُزْ ضِفْ ذَا نِعَمْ دَعْ سُوءَ ظَنٍّ زُرْ شَرِيفًا لِلْكَرَمْ
27.en: “Be good, then keep family ties and you will succeed; host a generous person; leave bad thoughts; visit the noble for honour.” The first letter of each word is one of the 14 Sun letters.

28.ar: وَاللَّامَ الْأُولَى سَمِّهَا قَمَرِيَّةْ وَاللَّامَ الْأُخْرَى سَمِّهَا شَمْسِيَّةْ
28.en: Call the first Lam Qamariyyah and call the other Lam Shamsiyyah.

29.ar: وَأَظْهِرَنَّ لَامَ فِعْلٍ مُطْلَقَا فِي نَحْوِ قُلْ نَعَمْ وَقُلْنَا وَالْتَقَى
29.en: Always pronounce the Lam of a verb clearly, as in Qul Na‘am, Qulna, and Iltaqa.

30.ar: إِنْ فِي الصِّفَاتِ وَالْمَخَارِجِ اتَّفَقْ حَرْفَانِ فَالْمِثْلَانِ فِيهِمَا أَحَقْ
30.en: When two letters agree in both qualities and articulation point, they are Mithlayn.

31.ar: وَإِنْ يَكُونَا مَخْرَجًا تَقَارَبَا وَفِي الصِّفَاتِ اخْتَلَفَا يُلَقَّبَا
31.en: When two letters are close in articulation but differ in qualities, they receive another classification.

32.ar: مُتَقَارِبَيْنِ أَوْ يَكُونَا اتَّفَقَا فِي مَخْرَجٍ دُونَ الصِّفَاتِ حُقِّقَا
32.en: They are Mutaqaribayn; if they share an articulation point but not their qualities, then they are different.

33.ar: بِالْمُتَجَانِسَيْنِ ثُمَّ إِنْ سَكَنْ أَوَّلُ كُلٍّ فَالصَّغِيرَ سَمِّيَنْ
33.en: They are Mutajanisayn; when the first of a pair is Sakin, call the meeting small.

34.ar: أَوْ حُرِّكَ الْحَرْفَانِ فِي كُلٍّ فَقُلْ كُلٌّ كَبِيرٌ وَافْهَمَنْهُ بِالْمُثُلْ
34.en: When both letters are vowelled, call the meeting large, and understand it through examples.

35.ar: وَالْمَدُّ أَصْلِيٌّ وَفَرْعِيٌّ لَهُ وَسَمِّ أَوَّلًا طَبِيعِيًّا وَهُوَ
35.en: Madd is primary and secondary; call the first type natural Madd.

36.ar: مَا لَا تَوَقُّفٌ لَهُ عَلَى سَبَبْ وَلَا بِدُونِهِ الْحُرُوفُ تُجْتَلَبْ
36.en: Natural Madd does not depend on a cause, and the Madd letters cannot exist correctly without it.

37.ar: بَلْ أَيُّ حَرْفٍ غَيْرُ هَمْزٍ أَوْ سُكُونْ جَا بَعْدَ مَدٍّ فَالطَّبِيعِيُّ يَكُونْ
37.en: If something other than Hamzah or Sukoon follows a Madd letter, the Madd is natural.

38.ar: وَالْآخَرُ الْفَرْعِيُّ مَوْقُوفٌ عَلَى سَبَبْ كَهَمْزٍ أَوْ سُكُونٍ مُسْجَلَا
38.en: The other type is secondary Madd, which depends on a cause such as Hamzah or Sukoon.

39.ar: حُرُوفُهُ ثَلَاثَةٌ فَعِيهَا مِنْ لَفْظِ وَايٍ وَهِيَ فِي نُوحِيهَا
39.en: The Madd letters are three; learn them from the word “Wāy,” and find them in “Nūḥīhā.”

40.ar: وَالْكَسْرُ قَبْلَ الْيَا وَقَبْلَ الْوَاوِ ضَمٌّ شَرْطٌ وَفَتْحٌ قَبْلَ أَلِفٍ يُلْتَزَمْ
40.en: Kasrah comes before Ya, Dammah before Waw, and Fathah before Alif.

41.ar: وَاللِّينُ مِنْهَا الْيَا وَوَاوٌ سُكِّنَا إِنِ انْفِتَاحٌ قَبْلَ كُلٍّ أُعْلِنَا
41.en: The letters of Leen are Ya and Waw with Sukoon when each is preceded by Fathah.

42.ar: لِلْمَدِّ أَحْكَامٌ ثَلَاثَةٌ تَدُومْ وَهِيَ الْوُجُوبُ وَالْجَوَازُ وَاللُّزُومْ
42.en: Madd has three rulings: Wajib, Ja’iz, and Lazim.

43.ar: فَوَاجِبٌ إِنْ جَاءَ هَمْزٌ بَعْدَ مَدْ فِي كِلْمَةٍ وَذَا بِمُتَّصِلٍ يُعَدْ
43.en: Madd is Wajib when Hamzah follows a Madd letter in the same word; this is Muttasil.

44.ar: وَجَائِزٌ مَدٌّ وَقَصْرٌ إِنْ فُصِلْ كُلٌّ بِكِلْمَةٍ وَهَذَا الْمُنْفَصِلْ
44.en: Madd may be lengthened or shortened when the Madd and Hamzah are in separate words; this is Munfasil.

45.ar: وَمِثْلُ ذَا إِنْ عَرَضَ السُّكُونُ وَقْفًا كَتَعْلَمُونَ نَسْتَعِينْ
45.en: The same choice applies when a temporary Sukoon appears because the reciter stops.

46.ar: أَوْ قُدِّمَ الْهَمْزُ عَلَى الْمَدِّ وَذَا بَدَلْ كَآمَنُوا وَإِيمَانًا خُذَا
46.en: When Hamzah comes before the Madd letter, it is Madd Badal, as in Amanu and Imanan.

47.ar: وَلَازِمٌ إِنِ السُّكُونُ أُصِّلَا وَصْلًا وَوَقْفًا بَعْدَ مَدٍّ طُوِّلَا
47.en: Madd is Lazim when a permanent Sukoon follows the Madd letter when joining and stopping.

48.ar: أَقْسَامُ لَازِمٍ لَدَيْهِمْ أَرْبَعَةْ وَتِلْكَ كِلْمِيٌّ وَحَرْفِيٌّ مَعَهْ
48.en: The scholars divide Madd Lazim into four types: Kalimi and Harfi are the two main groups.

49.ar: كِلَاهُمَا مُخَفَّفٌ مُثَقَّلُ فَهَذِهِ أَرْبَعَةٌ تُفَصَّلُ
49.en: Each of Kalimi and Harfi may be either Mukhaffaf or Muthaqqal, making four types.

50.ar: فَإِنْ بِكِلْمَةٍ سُكُونٌ اجْتَمَعْ مَعْ حَرْفِ مَدٍّ فَهْوَ كِلْمِيٌّ وَقَعْ
50.en: When Sukoon meets a Madd letter inside one word, it is Madd Lazim Kalimi.

51.ar: أَوْ فِي ثُلَاثِيِّ الْحُرُوفِ وُجِدَا وَالْمَدُّ وَسْطُهُ فَحَرْفِيٌّ بَدَا
51.en: When this occurs in a three-letter opening letter-name with Madd in its middle, it is Harfi.

52.ar: كِلَاهُمَا مُثَقَّلٌ إِنْ أُدْغِمَا مُخَفَّفٌ كُلٌّ إِذَا لَمْ يُدْغَمَا
52.en: Each type is Muthaqqal when merging occurs and Mukhaffaf when no merging occurs.

53.ar: وَاللَّازِمُ الْحَرْفِيُّ أَوَّلَ السُّوَرْ وُجُودُهُ وَفِي ثَمَانٍ انْحَصَرْ
53.en: Madd Lazim Harfi appears in the opening letters of Surahs and is limited to eight letters.

54.ar: يَجْمَعُهَا حُرُوفُ كَمْ عَسَلْ نَقَصْ وَعَيْنٌ ذُو وَجْهَيْنِ وَالطُّولُ أَخَصْ
54.en: The eight letters are gathered in “Kam ‘Asal Naqas”; Ayn has two accepted lengths, with the longer preferred here.

55.ar: وَمَا سِوَى الْحَرْفِ الثُّلَاثِيِّ لَا أَلِفْ فَمَدُّهُ مَدًّا طَبِيعِيًّا أُلِفْ
55.en: Other opening letters, apart from the three-part letters and Alif, are read with natural Madd.

56.ar: وَذَاكَ أَيْضًا فِي فَوَاتِحِ السُّوَرْ فِي لَفْظِ حَيٍّ طَاهِرٍ قَدِ انْحَصَرْ
56.en: The natural-Madd opening letters are gathered in the phrase “Hayyun Tahir.”

57.ar: وَيَجْمَعُ الْفَوَاتِحَ الْأَرْبَعْ عَشَرْ صِلْهُ سُحَيْرًا مَنْ قَطَعْكَ ذَا اشْتَهَرْ
57.en: The fourteen opening letters of the surahs are gathered in “silhu suhayran man qata‘ak” (join at dawn the one who cut you off). This is well known.

58.ar: وَتَمَّ ذَا النَّظْمُ بِحَمْدِ اللَّهِ عَلَى تَمَامِهِ بِلَا تَنَاهِي
58.en: This poem is completed with praise of Allah, fully and without end.

59.ar: أَبْيَاتُهُ نَدٌّ بَدَا لِذِي النُّهَى تَارِيخُهَا بُشْرَى لِمَنْ يُتْقِنُهَا
59.en: Its number of lines is “nadd bada” (61) for people of understanding, and its date is “bushra li-man yutqinuha” (good news for whoever masters it: the year 1198).

60.ar: ثُمَّ الصَّلَاةُ وَالسَّلَامُ أَبَدَا عَلَى خِتَامِ الْأَنْبِيَاءِ أَحْمَدَا
60.en: Then may blessings and peace remain forever upon Ahmad ﷺ, the final Prophet.

61.ar: وَالْآلِ وَالصَّحْبِ وَكُلِّ تَابِعِ وَكُلِّ قَارِئٍ وَكُلِّ سَامِعِ
61.en: And upon his family, companions, followers, every reciter, and every listener.
